title: Anxiety disorders, OCD and PTSD
blurb: Apply NICE stepped care for GAD and panic, ERP for OCD and trauma-focused therapy for PTSD, and avoid the treatments NICE warns against.
question: After a serious motorway crash, a hospital manager plans a group 'debriefing' session for all staff and survivors the next day to prevent PTSD. A nurse is asked for her view. What does NICE NG116 say?

teach.h: Anxiety is a family of conditions
teach.body: Generalised anxiety disorder (GAD) is persistent, excessive worry about many everyday things. Panic disorder involves recurrent unexpected panic attacks and fear of further attacks. OCD combines obsessions (intrusive unwanted thoughts) with compulsions (repeated acts to reduce the distress). PTSD follows trauma, with re-experiencing, avoidance and hyperarousal. In plain English: each has its own NICE pathway, and psychological therapy is central to all of them.

levels.label: Step 3: CBT, applied relaxation or SSRI

teach.caption: CG113 1.2.1: offer the least intrusive, most effective intervention first.

head: Condition
Drug choice
Avoid
rows: Then another SSRI or an SNRI
teach.caption: CG113 1.2.23-1.2.27, 1.3.20-1.3.26.

teach.body: For panic disorder, CBT is delivered by trained, supervised practitioners: 7 to 14 hours in total, usually weekly 1 to 2 hour sessions, completed within 4 months. Briefer CBT of about 7 hours is combined with structured self-help materials. Mild to moderate panic can start with self-help. Benzodiazepines are linked to worse long-term outcomes and should not be prescribed for panic disorder.

children.label: SSRI or intensive CBT with ERP

teach.caption: CG31 1.5.1.1-1.5.1.4. ERP = exposure and response prevention: facing the feared trigger without performing the compulsion.

teach.body: For adults with OCD the first SSRI is one of fluoxetine, fluvoxamine, paroxetine, sertraline or citalopram. If it works, continue for at least 12 months to prevent relapse. Clomipramine is considered after at least one SSRI has failed or was not tolerated. Children and young people with moderate to severe OCD are offered CBT including ERP that involves the family and is adapted to their age.

items.label: Subthreshold: active monitoring; ASD or marked symptoms: TF-CBT

teach.caption: NG116 1.6.4-1.6.19. TF-CBT and EMDR typically 8–12 sessions, more for multiple traumas.

teach.body: NICE says do not offer drug treatments, including benzodiazepines, to prevent PTSD in adults. For adults with PTSD who prefer drug treatment, consider venlafaxine or an SSRI such as sertraline, and review regularly. For children and young people under 18, do not offer drug treatment to prevent or treat PTSD; trauma-focused CBT is the main treatment.

Nurse Ward explains that NICE NG116 says do not offer psychologically-focused debriefing to prevent or treat PTSD. Instead she suggests practical support, information about normal reactions, and active monitoring for anyone with subthreshold symptoms, with follow-up within a month. People with acute stress disorder or clinically important symptoms are referred for individual trauma-focused CBT.

teach.text: 'Talking it through straight away' sounds kind, but psychologically-focused debriefing is NOT recommended for preventing PTSD. And benzodiazepines are not the answer for panic disorder or for preventing PTSD, however distressed the person is.

items: GAD: stepped care; high intensity = CBT or applied relaxation; SSRI with sertraline first.
Panic: CBT 7–14 hours; SSRI licensed for panic; no benzodiazepines.
OCD: CBT with ERP; moderate = SSRI or intensive CBT; severe = both; continue SSRI 12 months.
PTSD: no debriefing; TF-CBT; EMDR for non-combat trauma after 3 months (consider at 1–3).
No drugs to prevent PTSD; no PTSD drugs in under-18s.

summary: You can now apply NICE stepped care for GAD and panic disorder, match OCD treatment to impairment, and plan PTSD care with trauma-focused therapy. You know which treatments NICE advises against.

A.q: What does NICE NG116 say about psychologically-focused debriefing after a traumatic event?
options: Offer it within 72 hours to everyone exposed
Offer it to people with prior mental illness
Do not offer it to prevent or treat PTSD
Offer it in groups led by a trained peer
A.why: NG116 1.6.5: do not offer psychologically-focused debriefing for the prevention or treatment of PTSD.

whyNot.0: NICE recommends against debriefing at any time point.
whyNot.1: A mental health history does not make debriefing recommended.
whyNot.3: Group debriefing is still psychologically-focused debriefing.

A.q: Which drug does NICE CG113 suggest considering first for GAD?
A.why: CG113 1.2.23: if a person with GAD chooses drug treatment, offer an SSRI; consider sertraline first as the most cost-effective.

whyNot.0: Benzodiazepines are not offered for GAD except short-term in a crisis.
whyNot.1: Antipsychotics are not offered for GAD in primary care.
whyNot.2: Pregabalin is not the first choice in CG113.

A.q: What is the core technique in CBT for OCD?
A.why: CG31: CBT for OCD includes exposure and response prevention (ERP).

whyNot.1: Applied relaxation is a GAD option.

B.q: Josh, 32, has panic disorder and asks for diazepam to carry with him. What does NICE CG113 advise?
options: Prescribe it to carry for use during attacks
Prescribe it with an SSRI for 3 months
B.why: CG113 1.3.20: benzodiazepines are associated with a less good long-term outcome and should not be prescribed for panic disorder.

whyNot.0: PRN benzodiazepines are still not recommended for panic disorder.
whyNot.1: A short course is still a benzodiazepine prescription for panic.
whyNot.2: NICE does not recommend adding a benzodiazepine to an SSRI for panic.

B.q: Maya, 26, has OCD with moderate functional impairment. What does NICE CG31 recommend?
options: An SSRI or intensive CBT with ERP
B.why: CG31 1.5.1.3: adults with moderate impairment are offered a choice of an SSRI or more intensive CBT including ERP (more than 10 therapist hours).

whyNot.0: Low-intensity treatment is for mild impairment.
whyNot.2: Clomipramine is considered after an SSRI has failed.
whyNot.3: Adding an antipsychotic is for treatment-resistant cases after MDT review.

B.q: Dev, 40, was assaulted 5 months ago and now has PTSD from this non-combat trauma. He prefers EMDR. What does NICE recommend?
B.why: NG116 1.6.19: offer EMDR to adults with PTSD presenting more than 3 months after non-combat trauma.

whyNot.2: Benzodiazepines are not a PTSD treatment.
whyNot.3: Counselling is not the NICE trauma-focused therapy.

C.q: Sam, 15, has PTSD after a house fire 4 months ago. His parents ask about medication. What does NG116 advise?
C.why: NG116 1.6.14 and 1.6.11: do not offer drug treatments for PTSD in under-18s; offer individual trauma-focused CBT to 7 to 17-year-olds presenting more than 3 months after trauma.

whyNot.0: Drug treatment is not offered for PTSD in under-18s.
whyNot.1: Venlafaxine is an adult option only on preference, not for under-18s.
whyNot.3: Benzodiazepines are not offered for PTSD.

C.q: Carol, 50, has GAD. Guided self-help did not help and she now has marked functional impairment. She does not want medication. What is the next step?
options: Repeat guided self-help for another 6 weeks
A short course of a benzodiazepine
C.why: CG113 step 3: with inadequate response to step 2 or marked impairment, offer a choice of high-intensity psychological intervention (CBT or applied relaxation) or drug treatment; she prefers therapy.

whyNot.0: Repeating a failed low-intensity step does not follow stepped care.
whyNot.2: Inpatient care is step 4, for very marked impairment or high risk.
whyNot.3: Benzodiazepines are for short-term crisis use only.

C.q: Ian, 38, has OCD and has responded well to fluoxetine for 4 months. He wants to stop now. What does CG31 recommend?
options: Stop now, as he has responded
Halve the dose and stop in a week
C.why: CG31 1.5.3.15: if SSRI treatment for OCD is effective, continue for at least 12 months to prevent relapse and allow further improvement.

whyNot.2: Switching is for non-response, not a good response.
whyNot.3: This stops far too early and too fast.

reteach.title: One condition, one pathway
reteach.question: How do you remember what NICE recommends for each anxiety condition?

blocks.body: GAD: stepped care, CBT or applied relaxation, sertraline first. Panic: CBT 7 to 14 hours, SSRI, no benzodiazepines. OCD: CBT with ERP. PTSD: trauma-focused CBT or EMDR, no debriefing.

blocks.text: Debriefing straight after trauma is not recommended.

explain.body: Step 1: identify, educate, actively monitor. Step 2: low-intensity (self-help, guided self-help, groups). Step 3: CBT or applied relaxation, or an SSRI. Step 4: specialist care.

test.q: Which interventions sit at step 2 of the GAD stepped-care model?
options: Inpatient care and crisis team support
test.why: CG113: step 2 offers low-intensity interventions: non-facilitated self-help, guided self-help and psychoeducational groups.

explain.body: CBT 7 to 14 hours in total, weekly 1 to 2 hour sessions, within 4 months. SSRI licensed for panic; imipramine or clomipramine if no improvement after 12 weeks. No benzodiazepines, sedating antihistamines or antipsychotics.

test.q: What total duration of CBT does NICE recommend for panic disorder?
test.why: CG113 1.3.15: CBT in the optimal range of 7 to 14 hours in total should be offered.

whyNot.0: This is below the NICE range.
whyNot.2: This is above the NICE range.
whyNot.3: This is far above the NICE range.

explain.body: Mild: low-intensity CBT with ERP up to 10 therapist hours. Moderate: SSRI or intensive CBT with ERP. Severe: both. SSRIs: fluoxetine, fluvoxamine, paroxetine, sertraline or citalopram; continue at least 12 months if effective.

test.q: What does NICE CG31 recommend for an adult with OCD and severe functional impairment?
options: An SSRI plus CBT with ERP
test.why: CG31 1.5.1.4: adults with severe functional impairment are offered combined treatment with an SSRI and CBT including ERP.

whyNot.1: An SSRI by itself is a choice for moderate impairment.
whyNot.2: Clomipramine is considered after an SSRI fails.

explain.body: Adults: trauma-focused CBT (8 to 12 sessions). EMDR offered after 3 months for non-combat trauma. No drugs to prevent PTSD; venlafaxine or an SSRI if the person prefers drug treatment. Under-18s: no drugs.

test.q: An adult with PTSD prefers medication to therapy. Which does NICE suggest considering?
test.why: NG116 1.6.25: consider venlafaxine or an SSRI such as sertraline for adults with PTSD who prefer drug treatment, reviewed regularly.

whyNot.0: Benzodiazepines are not recommended for PTSD.
whyNot.2: Antipsychotics are not the NICE drug option for PTSD.
whyNot.3: Mood stabilisers are not PTSD treatments.
